claims.text: The proposed initial material is a single-phase CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with a uniform elemental distribution and minimal grain-boundary segregation.
Rapid quenching after solution treatment minimizes grain-boundary diffusion and segregation.
Slower post-solution-treatment cooling produces a subtle, measurable increase in grain-boundary segregation.
At elevated temperature, Cr, Ni, and Mn can segregate or form nanoclusters at CoCrFeMnNi grain boundaries.
Intermediate service temperatures can provide sufficient atomic mobility for segregation without causing large-scale precipitation.
Grain-boundary segregation or nanoclustering weakens local interfacial cohesion and promotes grain-boundary decohesion.
Segregation-induced weakening creates localized stress concentrations under mechanical load.
A critical grain-boundary segregation level exists above which boundaries become preferred sites for brittle crack nucleation.
Brittle grain-boundary failure can emerge in a nominally single-phase alloy even without conventional intermetallic precipitates.
Slow-cooled specimens will have lower ductility than rapidly quenched specimens under otherwise identical loading.
Slow-cooled specimens will initiate intergranular cracks earlier and show a more brittle fracture mode than rapidly quenched specimens.
The two cooling groups will initially deform similarly at low strain and then diverge when a critical stress is reached.
The rapidly quenched baseline retains minimal grain-boundary segregation.
The rapidly quenched baseline displays high ductility and toughness characteristic of a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
At very low temperatures, negligible diffusion makes segregation-driven embrittlement unlikely to dominate.
At very high temperatures, additional phase changes may make the proposed segregation mechanism non-dominant.
A rapid-quench versus slow-cooling comparison, combined with grain-boundary chemistry and mechanical-fracture measurements, can test the proposed causal chain.
Failure to detect either increased segregation or reduced ductility and increased intergranular cracking in the slow-cooled group is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: PMC9848264::web::000::abstract is designated as both supporting and conflicting evidence.

The hypothesis predicts that slow cooling causes embrittlement, whereas the cited Al-Co-Cr-Ni-Ti-Nb-Zr-B alloy study reports that slow cooling produces precipitate-assisted serrated grain boundaries and substantially improves fracture strain and creep life. That record therefore does not support the stated cooling-rate outcome and concerns a different alloy and mechanism.
